metrics.label: Brent crude
metrics.blurb: The global benchmark price for crude oil. Most oil cargoes price off it.
metrics.fallback: CNBC live quote, then the daily oil report, then EIA/FRED

metrics.label: WTI crude
metrics.blurb: The US crude benchmark. Its gap to Brent drives US export volumes.
metrics.fallback: CNBC live quote, then the daily oil report, then EIA/FRED

metrics.label: Dutch TTF gas
metrics.blurb: Europe's benchmark gas price, set in the Netherlands.
metrics.fallback: read from the daily European gas report

metrics.label: Henry Hub gas
metrics.blurb: The US benchmark gas price, set in Louisiana.

metrics.label: Coal API2 (ARA)
metrics.blurb: Price of coal delivered into northwest Europe. A dry bulk demand signal.
metrics.fallback: CNBC lists ICE API2 but returns it undated; nothing else free publishes it.
metrics.source: ICE API2 Rotterdam Coal via CNBC

metrics.label: Heating oil / gasoil
metrics.blurb: A refined product price that tracks what bunker fuel costs.
metrics.fallback: CNBC live quote (ULSD heating oil front-month)

metrics.label: RBOB gasoline
metrics.blurb: US gasoline price. Strong margins here pull product tankers west.

metrics.label: Dry bulk ETF (BDRY)
metrics.blurb: An ETF holding dry bulk freight futures. A rough daily read on bulker sentiment.
metrics.source: Breakwave Dry Bulk Shipping ETF via CNBC

metrics.label: Tanker ETF (BWET)
metrics.blurb: An ETF holding tanker freight futures. A rough daily read on tanker sentiment.
metrics.source: Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF via CNBC

metrics.label: Baltic Capesize Index
metrics.blurb: The Capesize component of the Baltic Dry Index. The most volatile part, and effectively a bet on Chinese steel production.

metrics.label: Baltic Panamax Index
metrics.blurb: The Panamax component. Coal and grain rather than iron ore, so it follows harvests and power demand more than steel.

metrics.label: Baltic Supramax Index
metrics.blurb: The Supramax component. These ships have their own cranes and serve smaller ports, so it reflects broad trade rather than one commodity.

metrics.label: Baltic Dry Index
metrics.blurb: The Baltic Exchange's headline dry bulk freight index. Published late afternoon London time, so a morning brief shows the previous session.
metrics.source: Baltic Exchange via Hellenic Shipping News

metrics.label: VLSFO Singapore
metrics.blurb: Price of the main low-sulphur marine fuel at the world's biggest bunker port.

metrics.label: VLSFO Rotterdam
metrics.blurb: The same fuel in Europe's biggest bunker port.

metrics.label: VLSFO Fujairah
metrics.blurb: The Middle East bunker hub, where most VLCC voyages refuel.

metrics.label: Diesel crack vs Brent
metrics.blurb: Roughly what a refinery makes turning a barrel of crude into diesel. Computed as the gasoil price converted to barrels minus Brent. Fat margins make refineries run hard, which creates product tanker cargo.

metrics.label: Brent–WTI spread
metrics.blurb: How much more Brent costs than WTI. A wide gap makes exporting US crude profitable, which means more long-haul cargoes and stronger tanker demand.

rates.label: VLCC (TD3C, AG→China)
rates.blurb: Daily earnings of a 2m-barrel crude tanker on the Arabian Gulf to China run. The most quoted tanker rate in the world.

rates.label: Suezmax (TD20, W.Africa→UKC)
rates.blurb: Daily earnings of a 1m-barrel crude tanker from West Africa to Europe.

rates.label: Aframax (TD7, N.Sea→UKC)
rates.blurb: Daily earnings of a 600k-barrel crude tanker on a short North Sea haul — the route closest to Norwegian crude exports.

rates.label: LR2 (TC1, AG→Japan)
rates.blurb: Daily earnings of a large product tanker carrying clean refined products.

brief.text:
The most important thing in today's data is what is missing: no freight benchmark has refreshed. Every dry bulk index and every tanker, LNG and LPG time-charter equivalent figure — TCE, the daily dollar earnings a ship makes on a voyage after voyage costs — carries an older date. The only live numbers this morning are crude, gas, products and bunker fuel. If you are quoting a rate today, you are quoting Thursday's dry indices at best, and in the tanker market numbers from five or more sessions ago, so treat them as background rather than as the market's current level.

On today's figures, Brent crude is 92.62 dollars a barrel, up 0.64 (+0.7%), WTI is 83.33, up 0.12 (+0.1%), leaving the Brent–WTI spread at 9.29 dollars. Henry Hub US gas is 3.22 dollars per mmBtu, down 1.4%. The striking move is in VLSFO, the low-sulphur fuel oil ships burn: Rotterdam is up 10 dollars to 715 a tonne and Singapore up 3 to 834, while Fujairah is down 19.50 to 803 (-2.4%) and Houston down 22.50 to 722.50 (-3.0%). Crude up and two bunker hubs down sharply is an unusual split, and the data here does not show why. The diesel crack — refining margin over Brent — stands at 73.59 dollars a barrel today, with no change figure given. For reference only: the Baltic Dry Index, the composite dry bulk freight benchmark, was 2,901 points on Thursday 19 November, down 13 (-0.4%), with the Capesize index (largest bulkers, typically iron ore and coal) at 4,514, down 35.

Running stories: a US congressional committee is urging sanctions over China's detention of Panama-flagged ships, which develops the live dispute around US port fees on Chinese-built and Chinese-operated tonnage. The Hormuz attacks, Russian refinery damage and diesel export limits, shadow-fleet sanctions, Black Sea strikes and the threatened strike at Los Angeles–Long Beach all had no fresh news in today's data and are unchanged. Trade press reports weekly dry bulk gains of 8.6% for the Capesize index and 5.7% for Panamax, concentrated on Atlantic routes.

Watch two things. First, whether the Baltic indices and tanker TCEs refresh, since the Thursday dry prints and the 15 November tanker prints are the oldest part of your picture. Second, whether the Fujairah and Houston bunker falls extend or reverse, because bunkers are a direct voyage cost in every calculation you run.

storylines.title: Attacks and escalation around Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue. The LPG tanker TARA GAS remained on fire and adrift off Oman after an attack that left 11 injured, and US guidance has widened a blockade to cover vessels loading Iranian cargo at sea.
storylines.why_it_matters: Hull strikes and blockade guidance raise war-risk premiums for Arabian Gulf liftings, slow transits and shrink the pool of willing owners, reshaping crude, product and gas ton-miles.

storylines.title: Attacks on shipping in the Black Sea
storylines.what: Drone strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea have continued through November, with two vessels sunk off Bulgaria and crew injured following an earlier wheat carrier capsizing.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling in the region.

storylines.title: Russian refining damage and diesel export limits
storylines.what: Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian refineries' combined crude processing by 45% since late October, on top of a Russian ban on most diesel exports extended to end-January and contested reports of a US-Russia diesel arrangement.
storylines.why_it_matters: Lost Russian refining and export restrictions reshape clean product ton-miles, pulling diesel from longer-haul sources and changing MR and LR employment and crude export balances.

storylines.title: Sanctions and evasion in the shadow fleet
storylines.what: Sanctions pressure on the shadow fleet is widening, with EU measures targeting shipowners, managers, insurers and financial networks, adding to earlier US designations.
storylines.why_it_matters: Designations force charterers and underwriters to re-verify counterparties, documents and vessel positions, and can strand tonnage outside compliant trade.

storylines.title: US-China ship fees and port state control friction
storylines.what: The US has extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months while trade talks continue. A US congressional committee is now urging sanctions over China's detention of Panama-flagged ships.
storylines.why_it_matters: Reinstated fees, sanctions or retaliatory detentions would change the cost and risk of deploying particular tonnage into US and Chinese trades and affect chartering preferences across sectors.
storylines.latest: A US congressional committee is urging sanctions over China's detention of Panama-flagged ships, escalating the dispute beyond the suspended port fees.
sources: US Committee Urges Sanctions Over China’s Detention of Panama-Flagged Ships

storylines.title: Strike threat at LA-Long Beach
storylines.what: The Los Angeles-Long Beach port complex is bracing for a strike, with employers warning of severe supply chain disruption if last-ditch talks fail.
storylines.why_it_matters: A stoppage at the largest US West Coast gateway would disrupt container flows, berth availability and inland logistics, with knock-on congestion for vessels scheduled to call.
